title: The Ice Cream Truck Doctrine
text: The ice cream truck's song drifts down the street. {kid} freezes, then turns to you with the face of someone whose ship has come in.

choices.label: "It only plays music when it's out of ice cream."

outcomes.text: {kid} takes this in, nods gravely and waves goodbye to the sad, empty truck. It's the cleanest win of your career. You have just written a check.
It melts down {kid}'s arm, both sleeves and the stroller. Pure joy, then stickiness, in that order.
They want the one on the poster. The one on the poster was discontinued years ago. The truck leaves. The poster stays in their heart.
"Weekend food," they repeat, filing it with the other laws. They will enforce it on you Saturday at 7 AM.
The truck turns the corner. The song fades. The scream does not.

title: The Truck Comes Back
text: The truck is back, song blaring. {kid} waves sadly: "Bye, empty truck." Then the neighbor's kid runs out, comes back with an ice cream sandwich and takes a slow bite, staring straight at your window.

outcomes.text: {kid} accepts this. Your lie now has a sequel. By Thursday it will need a prequel and a map.
"Then why is the music ON?" They've found the flaw in the doctrine. The investigation will be ongoing. The scream is immediate.
You catch the truck at the corner. {kid} gets the ice cream and full knowledge of what you are. They eat it while watching you, the way the neighbor's kid did.

choices.label: Close the blinds. "Who wants a BATH?"

outcomes.text: Nobody wants a bath. Behind the blinds, the song plays on for eleven more minutes.
"BATH!" It works. They sprint for the tub. You have discovered the only thing that beats ice cream, and it's the thing they fought last night.

title: Just Lie Down for a Minute
text: Dinner's over. The dishes are a tower. {partner} is scrubbing the high chair tray. The couch is right there, humming a song only you can hear.

choices.label: Lie down. Just for one minute.

outcomes.text: You lie down for a minute. The minute lasts 20. It's the best minute of your month.
You wash. You stack. You narrate your own sacrifice in your head, in the voice of a nature documentary.
You do every dish. At 9 PM {partner} says, "Oh, you did the dishes?" in the tone people use when you take up the harp.
You wash, they dry. Neither of you mentions the toddler. It feels like a small, damp date.

title: Very Loud Dishes
text: You open your eyes to the sound of {partner} doing the dishes. Loudly. Each plate goes into the rack like a closing argument.

choices.label: Get up, grab a towel, say thank you

outcomes.text: "Thanks for doing these." "Mm." You dry in silence. The silence is itemized.
"Thanks for doing these." They hand you a plate and, after a second, bump your hip with theirs. Forgiven. Mostly.

choices.label: "I was up at five with them."

outcomes.text: "I was up at five too. Then I went to work." A pan goes into the rack with real feeling. Nobody wins this one. Not even the pan.

choices.label: Stay horizontal. Commit to the bit.

outcomes.text: You keep your eyes shut. They know you're awake. You know they know. The dishes get done, and filed, and remembered.
You fake a snore. Too big. A cartoon snore. {partner} laughs so hard they have to sit on the kitchen floor. You've never been forgiven so fast for something so bad.

title: "Playground?"
text: {kid} is holding out your shoes and pointing at the door. "Playground?" It's drizzling. You're wearing one sock. The sock isn't yours.

outcomes.text: "Later" works like a spell. They put the shoes down. You sit. You have just taken out a loan at a rate a payday lender would call aggressive.

choices.label: Go now. Find a second sock.

outcomes.text: Slide, wet bench, slide, for 45 minutes. Their cheeks go pink. You hold your coffee by the swings, as a hand warmer, which is all it is now.
The playground is closed for "resurfacing." {kid} stares through the fence at the slide. You have invented a new kind of sad.
They drop the shoes and wander off to bother a block tower. You suspect a trap. There is no trap. You fold an entire load of laundry, stunned.
They lie face-down on the doormat in protest. A sit-in. They've unionized, and the union is one person, and it is lying on your shoes.

title: "Later" Is Now
text: Two hours ago you said "later." {kid} did not forget. {kid} never forgets anything you'd like them to. They're at the door in one shoe and your hat. "IT'S LATER."

outcomes.text: You go: tired, cold and later. They don't care. They run at the slide like it owes them money. Worth it, barely, then completely.
"You SAID." They're right. You did. This meltdown has the moral high ground, and it knows it.
"Later later" buys you 90 more minutes. They empty the shoe rack in protest. Your credit score with this toddler is now in the low hundreds.
"Later later is NOW," they rule, citing nothing, and hand you the other shoe. You've been out-argued by someone who can't open a yogurt.

title: Fourteen People Ahead of You
text: The post office: fourteen people ahead of you and one window open. {kid} has started introducing themselves to other people's packages. "Hi, box."

outcomes.text: Silence, instantly. The woman behind you mouths "same." The line moves. Nobody has to know what this costs yet.
A stamp, a sad plant, a man holding nine identical boxes. By the window, {kid} is narrating for the whole line. Two people clap. The clerk does not.
"I spy something... YOU." They spy you eleven times in a row. It's still somehow the best option you had.

choices.label: Abandon the line. Mail it never.

outcomes.text: You leave. The package rides home in the stroller basket, where it will live for another week, judging you.

title: You Need Your Phone Back
text: In 15 minutes they've changed your phone's language to Finnish, taken 212 photos of their own nostril and texted your boss a single "p." They will not be returning it.

choices.label: Take it back. Brace for impact.

outcomes.text: You pry it loose. The scream has a bridge and a key change. Everyone in the post office is a witness now, and two of them are filming.
You hold out your hand. They hand it over. Just like that. A stranger looks at you like you're a wizard. You will never understand them.
Five more minutes. You both know what five more minutes is. It's a down payment on this exact fight.

choices.label: Trade it for your car keys

outcomes.text: The keys are accepted after a review period. You get the phone back, sticky forever. The keys vanish. You find them 40 minutes later in a boot.
They take the keys and press the red button. Outside, your car starts screaming. {kid} is thrilled. The post office is not. You've traded one alarm for a louder one.

title: Just Resting My Eyes
text: 3 PM, the dead zone. {kid} is next to you on the couch, "reading" a board book upside down, out loud. You could close your eyes. Just to listen better.

choices.label: Close your eyes. Just to listen.

outcomes.text: You're not asleep. You're listening with your eyes closed. You're listening so hard you drool a little.

choices.label: Get up. Walk around the block together.

outcomes.text: Cold air, one stick, one extremely important leaf. You come back more awake than you left. They come back sleepier. Everyone wins.
The walk takes 25 minutes and covers 40 feet. They found an ant. The ant was the walk.
The third coffee of the day tastes like a decision you'll revisit at 1 AM.

title: The Couch Hangover
text: The little rest is billing you. Your head is full of wet sand, a couch seam is printed across your cheek, and your body is now certain it's bedtime. It isn't even dinner.

choices.label: Cold water on your face. Push through.

outcomes.text: Cold water, a head shake and a pep talk in the mirror, which you lose. You get through the afternoon at about 60% of a person.
Coffee at 4 PM. The fog lifts. You can already hear it at 1 AM, knocking politely on the inside of your skull.
You lie back down. {kid} narrates the living room's destruction like a sports announcer. The cushions are gone. You hear the word "marker."
You wake at 5:15 with {kid} asleep on your chest, which is lovely, and a disaster. Bedtime just moved to 10 PM.

title: The Sticker Spa
text: {kid} has a sheet of 48 stickers and would like to "make you pretty." It's 20 quiet minutes. You'd only have to lie very still, and you're very good at lying still.

outcomes.text: Twenty glorious minutes of tiny hands patting your face. You may have dozed. You definitely relaxed. You did not check a mirror.
They put all 48 on one sheet of paper in a single, furious layer, glaring at you. It's a protest piece. It's honestly strong.
They put all 48 on the TV screen instead. It's paper-adjacent. You don't have the energy to argue the definition.

choices.label: Sticker them back. Spa for two.

outcomes.text: Matching star cheeks and a dinosaur on each nose. It's the most fun either of you has had all day. You peel yours off before the mail comes.

title: You Have Been Decorated
text: You catch your reflection in the microwave door: nine stickers, a cartoon pickle on one eyelid and a gold POTTY STAR in the middle of your forehead. The spa was an hour ago.

outcomes.text: The mail carrier. The neighbor. Eleven coworkers on video, for 40 minutes. Nobody said anything. That's either kindness or a group decision.
You wear them to pickup. Two parents compliment your "look." One asks where you got the pickle. You have never been more respected.
You wear them to pickup. Brynn looks at the POTTY STAR, then at you, then types something into a phone.
